speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to direct a question to the Minister of Labour? Will the minister inform the house as to what methods the government is using to secure personnel for employment on the St. Lawrence seaway? Second, has the minister's attention been drawn to the fact that a private organization, with headquarters in Cornwall, Ontario, is sending out circulars asking the unemployed to make application for employment on the seaway and to send $1 back to them with the application?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
speechtext:
I am grateful to my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South for giving me notice of his question, and I am glad to have an opportunity to reply to it.
The officials of the unemployment insurance commission have reported to me information regarding two private organizations such as that to which my hon. friend has referred. One of them goes under the name of "Seaway Opportunities" which asks for a fee of $1 to accompany the application for a job, and that I know is the one to which my hon. friend refers. The second one goes under the name of "International Recruiting Agency" which asks for a fee of $3. Both of these organizations give Cornwall post office addresses.
I have answered the last part of my hon. friend's question first. As to the first part of his question, concerning the method the government is using in helping to secure personnel for employment on the projects associated with both Ontario hydro and the
Inquiries of the Ministry federal seaway on the St. Lawrence, may I say that ever since the beginning our labour and national employment service officials have participated in the planning with regard to all matters related to future employment on both these projects. I believe that good methods have been worked out both as as they apply to the recruitment of workers within Canada and also to simplifying the movement of workers to and fro across the international border to ensure the maximum employment for Canadians and to best serve the changing needs of these great developments.
The St. Lawrence seaway authority in a press release yesterday stated that no outside organization had been authorized to indicate that they were acting as an agent for the seaway, and I have been assured by Mr. Chevrier that at one of its recent meetings the authority had approved the recommendation that the national employment service undertake recruiting for the seaway project. The local offices of the national employment service have been asked to advise all applicants in their areas who apply for positions on the seaway to register at their local office, and not to leave for a project until they are sure that work is available. These registrations will be passed on to a control office in the seaway area, and as contractors require workers applicants who meet the requirements of a particular job will be so advised and will then proceed to the project. Preference will be given to local residents if they are otherwise qualified.
At the present time, with the co-operation of the Ontario hydro commission, a refresher course is being conducted at Cornwall to bring national employment officers up to date on the requirements of the heavy construction industry. This program of training will be extended as the need for workers and the field for recruitment grows.
A moment ago I referred to the co-operation provided by Mr. Chevrier and the seaway authority. Here I should like to pay warm tribute to the valuable co-operation given to my officials and myself by the late Bob Saunders in planning this employment program, and for the continuing help of the Ontario hydro officials.
Through the courtesy of the Post Office Department, the national employment service is arranging to have posted in post offices throughout the country notices advising job seekers to check with their local employment office before proceeding to points where projects are contemplated.
The unemployment insurance commission will release to the press, trade journals and

Inquiries of the Ministry other publications, information covering the arrangements they have made to serve the needs of the seaway and power projects. The commission will continue to urge workers to see their local offices before they leave their home areas for any project, in order that they may be assured that work is available when they arrive there. I should like to underline the fact that the facilities of the national employment service are available to both workers and employers at no charge to them. It is, of course, the policy of the national employment service to give equal attention to the applications of workers whether or not they are covered by unemployment insurance.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in addition to press releases and other publicity on this matter during recent weeks, our national employment service has sent very specific instructions through the five regional offices to all the approximately 200 local offices across the country. If I may, since it is not too long, I should like to quote the exact words of that directive dated January 20 last, entitled "Recruitment for St. Lawrence Seaway and Hydro Project". It is signed by the director of employment services in Ottawa. This is the text:
Arrangements have been completed for us to do the recruiting for the above-mentioned projects. Details of procedure, etc., have not yet been completed but they will be sent out to the field in due course.
It is intended that we will have a central control office at Cornwall where the needs of the employers will be registered and requests will be made to our local offices for help as the occasion arises.
In so far as the hydro project is concerned, they are committed to the hiring of Ontario residents and particularly local residents in the area of the project, if these workers are suitable.
The seaway authorities tell us that they will give preference to local residents if they are suitable.
In order to be sure that the towns and cities where the projects are located are not swamped with people coming to look for a job, we have agreed to do everything possible to stop this.
Will you please, therefore, advise all offices in your region to post notices to the effect that residents are warned not to proceed to the seaway or hydro projects on the St. Lawrence without first being advised by our local offices. Any local publicity that can be given in this regard in the meantime would be beneficial.
Applications at our local offices should be carefully taken on a 701, obtaining all the information possible regarding the applicant, and these 701's should be kept readily available in the local office and the applicant advised not to proceed to the area until told to do so.
We hope to get out early next week a national news release outlining this arrangement. In the meantime, it is important that our offices at least be advised of what is being considered.
That is the end of the directive. I have taken the time of the house to answer this question fully because I know all members


of the house are as anxious as the hon. member for Cape Breton South or the Minister of Labour about this matter. I express the hope that the answer I have made be given wide publicity so that unemployed people in any part of the country might not be misled on the one hand or miss any real opportunity for employment on the other.

I was advised about 33 years ago when I first went into a government never to give a legal opinion, but to advise the inquirer to consult a lawyer. subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
The chief opposition to this bill respecting the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements seems to revolve around a specific project, the Kaiser dam. In the words of the spokesman of the Social Credit party, their opposition has a political basis, together with the assertion that it is an infringement on the rights of the provinces. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) said, as reported at page 886 of Hansard:
I am going to refer to the political aspects of the bill. My great opposition to the bill is that I believe it is nothing more or less than a political instrument used by the government of Canada to thwart the province of British Columbia in a development which the people have a right to expect.
Any act passed in this house, Mr. Speaker, naturally is a political act. I cannot see how it can be otherwise. It is an act of parliament and cannot be divorced from the question
International Rivers
of politics. It seems to me that the art of government can be defined as political.
The Social Credit party seems to be very sensitive when it comes to the question of political criticism. If any criticism is directed toward that party they immediately imply that it is a smear, or mud-slinging, and so on. It seems they can even change toothpaste into mud and imply that it has been thrown at some politician or other. I simply refer to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke and his statement at page 886. He took exception to the fact that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) mentioned the bright smile of the premier of British Columbia. I cannot see that there was any smearing done there. I warn the hon. member, who seems to feel injured and is jealous of the shiny, bright smile of the premier of British Columbia, that bright and shiny teeth are no facade for a virtuous personality. I need only refer him to the fable of Little Red Riding Hood.
It seems that the Conservative party, or at least the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), has in some way or other also developed the smear psychosis of the Social Credit party. In his inconsistent statement respecting this matter the hon. member said, on the one hand, that it was a political club to be used by the federal government to beat the provincial government of British Columbia, and on the other hand that he believed both parties were well-meaning and that their intentions were sincere. He cannot have it both ways. Therefore I think we can just disregard the official opposition and simply say that so far they are on the fence and are not taking any particular position at this time.
In his speech on Friday, which he concluded on Tuesday, the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke spoke, I presume, on behalf of the Social Credit party. I am concerned, as a matter of fact, over the hon. member's appalling ignorance of the facts respecting the Columbia river basin and the geography of British Columbia in general. For him to have drawn the conclusion that this is a political bill introduced for the purpose of injuring another party, when he has so little knowledge of the facts, is just beyond my comprehension.
It would be well to review some of the facts with respect to international treaties. I refer specifically to the treaty that was signed in 1909 between Canada and the United States. It was a treaty between His Majesty and the United States of America, signed on January 11, 1909. Under article 9 of that treaty the international joint commission was

International Rivers
given specific authority to deal with major questions arising in boundary disputes between the two great countries. Subsequently, in June, 1944, I believe, the matter of the development of the Columbia basin was referred to this commission. In a statement to the house at that time the late Right. Hon. Mackenzie King had this to say with respect to the reference as reported in Hansard of March 9, 1944, at page 1292:
As questions concerning the Columbia river basin are of great interest to the province of British Columbia, the government of that province has been consulted at all stages in the drafting of this reference.
Of course, such reference was to determine the best method of employing the water resources of the Columbia basin. There has been close co-operation between the federal authorities and the provincial governments in all phases of the investigation, at least up to the present moment. One of the first projects on which there was sufficient information available to proceed with was the Libby dam in Montana. While the investigation was not completed, the international joint commission was prepared to recommend the construction of the Libby dam which would build up one million kilowatts of on-site power with about 6 million kilowatts of energy in the combined on-site and downstream benefits. There was no decision, however, as to the benefits which would be paid to Canada in compensation for flooding north of the boundary in the area known as the Newgate district. About 42 miles of Canadian soil would be flooded and a considerable dislocation of residents would ensue. The United States section of the joint commission agreed only to $7 million in compensation, without any power in return. That is, there was to be no block of power which the Canadian section of the international joint commission felt should be returnable to Canada in perpetuity.
All the information available was given to the provincial authorities, but no decision was arrived at. Of course that recommendation had to be turned down as improper compensation for the use of our resources and storage space. As a result of the investigation by the Canadian section of the international joint commission they became convinced that Canada should be paid on a 50-50 basis for all downstream benefits from water stored in Canada. As was pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he opened this debate, that 50-50 basis is considered fair in that there must be flow as well as head, Canada providing the flow. I believe he is perfectly correct. The international joint commission's recommendation, we suggest, could be followed advisedly by all Canadian authorities.

of power, with a value of $840,000. Of course there would be other compensating factors in the way of taxes and so on. It has been ascertained that the diversion to the Fraser river would provide between two and three million kilowatts of on-site power and downstream benefits, which at the rate of $20 per kilowatt would total some $50 million as an annual return.
This is not to say that at some time or other, in years of excessive run-off, there may not be sufficient water to fill the storage at Mica creek as well as the storage in the Arrow lakes. Engineering studies have shown that it would be doubtful that there would be sufficient water for both these storage areas. If the lower one on the Arrow lakes is built first it would naturally have priority and would endanger the economics of the Mica creek project. What is even more important, it seems to me, is that the Mica creek diversion to the Fraser has become of great interest to electrical companies in Canada. The very fact that United States interests realize that we may use this surplus water in Canada gives them a different outlook when we are negotiating for downstream benefits.
Only yesterday I received a copy of the agreement between the Kaiser Aluminum company and the government of British Columbia. I cannot say that it is absolutely wrong that such an agreement should be drawn. I am not making that assertion. But certainly any 80-20 split is not what has been anticipated by those studying the project, and therefore in that regard alone it does not seem to be a satisfactory agreement even for 3 million acre feet under storage.
In searching through the agreement I am unable to find any reference whatsoever to any firm commitment between the Bonneville Power Corporation, which is the wholesaler of the power, and the Kaiser Aluminum company which has made an agreement with the province of British Columbia. That may be an oversight. I am not a lawyer, but I have drawn up an occasional agreement, and if I were responsible for drawing up a wage agreement I would certainly want it set out fairly clearly who was going to pay the wages or who has the responsibility of seeing to it that this block of power be retained in perpetuity? A company might well go bankrupt, and it seems to me that the word or seal of the United States government or one of its corporations would be essential to such an agreement.
The entire undertaking seems to undermine the far greater interests of the people in the Columbia basin. I have already pointed

In this case "downstream", of course, is in Idaho in the United States of America.
I happen to live in the area where the Kootenay river leaves Canada, flows into Montana, through Idaho, back into Canada, and into Kootenay lake, where it is stored, and where the West Kootenay Power company have framed a great amount of power. The water flows into the lower Kootenay, where it is gathered in a series of dams, one providing power for the city of Nelson and I believe owned by that city, and the others being utilized by the West Kootenay Power company. Oddly enough, this water flows into the Kootenay river just about the spot where the Kaiser Aluminum corporation proposes to build a dam on the Columbia. From there it flows into the United States through Washington and of course into Bonneville project, the Grand Coulee dam.
The hon. member stated that this was comparable to the Kaiser deal. But this application to which I have referred was made by the West Kootenay Power company during the days of the depression, when there was an abundance of power in the United States. At that time there was no thought of downstream benefits. Perhaps I should add, without reflecting on the earlier chairman, that we did not then have General McNaughton representing Canadian interests on the international joint commission.
However, during those depression years there was no demand for storage in Canada and, as a matter of fact, the West Kootenay Power and Light Company were required to pay damages to people living in the Bonners Ferry area in Idaho because the development slightly increased the danger of flooding in that district. It has also been claimed that this is an infringement on provincial rights. But I would like to know since when the present provincial government became so touchy about provincial rights. I have in my hand a brief prepared by Mr. Carl Goldenberg, Q.C., special counsel, and entitled "A Brief Submitted to the Government of Canada by the Government of British Columbia on Federal-Provincial Co-operation in Economic Development." We all knew the government was going to introduce legislation at this session. I think the reason this matter has been raised now, because of the development in British Columbia, is that for the first time in the history of our dominion a province has challenged what the federal government apparently took to be a right. Therefore they have found out that even under their existing legislation they need either clarification or additional power. Knowing that this matter was to be raised; knowing that I would get the viewpoint, the facts and the reasoning of the federal government as to why they brought in this legislation, I felt it was my duty as a member of the House of Commons from the province of British Columbia to go over to Victoria and point out to the government that, as a British Columbia M.P., when I arrived down here and heard the story of the federal government I should also have the facts and the point of view of the provincial government, and that if I did not get that information I would be placed in a most invidious position.
I went to see the premier of British Columbia and explained the situation. He said he would make an appointment for me with the minister of lands and forests. I had a long interview with Mr. Sommers, the minister of lands and forests, and I now feel I have the picture. I should like to outline it very

briefly, because it is important and because it definitely emphasizes the viewpoint of the provincial government, a different party from my own, which gives rise to what may be a constitutional problem.
As I have already stated British Columbia, for reasons best known to that government, signed an agreement with the Kaiser corporation on September 17, 1954. Under the terms of this agreement the corporation had to post $125,000 as a guarantee that they would proceed with all the test borings and so on. They were committed to spending not less than $100,000 before March 1 of this year, only some two and one-half weeks away. If, as a result of those borings, it was found feasible to establish a dam approximately six miles from Castlegar, then the corporation agreed to establish a Canadian corporation which would apply for a conditional water licence. If they got the conditional licence they would post an additional bond of $125,000. They would start construction of the dam on or before August 1, 1956 and would complete it by August 1, 1959.
By following through on this agreement the province of British Columbia would have built a dam financed by the Kaiser corporation at a cost somewhere between $25 million and $30 million. The province would receive 20 per cent of the power output delivered anywhere on the international border that the British Columbia government requested. The provincial government would receive annual taxes on the dam in the amount of approximately $275,000.
Now, at this point I asked the minister a question. May I say that I am not divulging any confidences; I went there officially as an M.P. from British Columbia, and in all the discussion I was told only once that something was in confidence. What I was told in confidence I cannot and will not disclose. There were no limitations placed on me concerning anything else I was told. One of the first questions I asked was the matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) a few moments ago. What is the relationship in this matter with the Bonneville power authority? The minister told me they had seen the agreement signed between the Kaiser corporation and the Bonneville power interests. Although there is no mention of that in the contract, such an agreement is in existence.
Having been told that this was the purpose of the original' agreement, I then stated that the government at Ottawa said the province would not be allowed to carry out this agreement. What was the position of the province? I want to convey to you the information I received because I think it is of interest and

of concern. The answer was, "We have a plan B, and if we cannot proceed with plan A because of the action of the federal government we will proceed with plan B." What is plan B? Plan B is that instead of the Kaiser corporation building the dam it will be built by the British Columbia power commission, which will borrow money under its government guarantee.
I cannot give you the exact amount, because the minister of lands and forests has mentioned three different figures in the last two months. He told me they would borrow at 3-75 per cent, but I noticed last week in his speech in the British Columbia legislature he said they would borrow at 4-2 per cent. If they borrow at 4-2 per cent, I believe they have an agreement with the Kaiser people that they will be paid back at the rate of 6-275 per cent. In other words, according to the minister of lands and forests, under plan B the provincial government would be making an additional gain because they would get the difference between 4-2 per cent and 6-275 per cent, at which rate they would be repaid by the Kaiser corporation. In addition, they would still get their 20 per cent of the power; they would still get their $275,000 in taxes, even although the dam would not be owned by Kaiser. Kaiser would make the province an annual grant of $275,000 as though the corporation owned it. In addition, the Kaiser people would make the provincial government a grant of somewhere between $250,000 and $350,000 annually to take care of the maintenance and improvements required on the dam owned by the British Columbia power commission.
That was plan B, which I understand they still intend to put into effect. This gave rise, sir, to the next question: If Ottawa passes an act to the effect that you have not the constitutional power, what are you going to do about it? The answer I received, and the answer I have read in the newspapers, is that the provincial government will challenge the authority of the federal government and will proceed with the dam.

And I could make a pretty good speech on the opposite side of the picture as well. I heard what the minister said. I was not going to comment upon it, but the only time he does not think I make a good speech is when he does not like what I am saying but does not know how to disagree with it.
If we look at section 92 of the British North America Act we can have no doubt whatsoever that matters such as we are now discussing come within the jurisdiction of the dominion government. We find that subsection 10(c) is as follows:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are ot the following classes:
(a) Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
That is pretty clear. It states that the province does not have jurisdiction if the federal parliament declares a work inside a province to be for the general good of Canada or of two or more of the provinces. But, sir, I was most interested to note that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke the other day he made reference to the treaty of 1909, which has been quoted by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). Although the hon. member quoted article 9 the Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted article 2. I may have misunderstood the minister, but I cannot interpret article 2 as giving exclusive power to the dominion government on international waters.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: That is what he said.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
That was the way I heard it, but if I am wrong I stand to be corrected. The minister made specific reference to article 2 which states this, very definitely:
Each of the high contracting parties reserves to itself, or to the several state governments on the one side and the dominion or provincial governments on the other-
And so on. I am not going to read all of it, but article 2 in the treaty of 1909, which is found in the statutes of 1911, does make reference to the provinces as well as to the dominion.
Now, British Columbia has been exercising powers in respect of international rivers for a good many years, under the authority of an act of the legislature. That authority is the water act of British Columbia, which has been on the statute books of the province since 1897. It was never yet been challenged, nor has there been any challenge of the authority exercised under it. To the best of

my knowledge British Columbia is now exercising a right it has always had, or that it has had since 1897.
But, sir, until now the federal government has never obstructed or objected to the use of that power. We are now discussing a general bill which, actually, has only one specific application at the moment, and that is to the Kaiser dam. It must be kept in mind, however, that the Columbia river takes in not only the Columbia river proper but takes in also all its tributaries and the lakes which go to make up the Columbia river basin. This takes in the Okanagan lakes, the Arrow lakes and the Kootenay lakes as well as numerous rivers and hundreds of creeks. And, sir, the Columbia river basin already has numerous dams, used not only for the purpose of generating power but for water storage and the water is stored not only for the benefit of British Columbia but for that of the United States. Objection has not been raised in the past; therefore I think it is understandable why confusion has now developed with the introduction of this bill, at a time when one more dam is going in.
I am trying only to give an outline of the picture as I see it. I believe a major constitutional issue is involved, or at least that the matter is in need of clarification. I am convinced we are not going to be able to settle the problem here or in Victoria. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce has in mind, I do believe that it will have to be referred to the supreme court. It might be a good idea if that announcement were made now so we could have a finding and an authoritative decision as to the constitutional rights, the position of the province and the dominion, and the distribution of authority between those two legislative bodies. It is necessary, because there does need to be clarification of the terminology of the constitution itself.
Under the British North America Act the province has control of its own natural resources. It is thought by many-I think I can say by most-that water is a natural resource of the province, and as long as the province deals only with that water inside its own borders it is a matter for provincial jurisdiction. The water actually does not come up for export until it leaves the province. The water eventually has to leave the province. Is the province therefore interfering with the export of water because it is on a controlled basis?
Until now the government has not taken the position that it now desires to take. Until now, as I understand it, the federal

government has taken the position that where the export comes in is not on the natural resource of water but on the export of power produced by the water inside the provincial boundary. That is quite obvious if you recall that not so long ago the government at Ottawa raised no objection-at least it must have agreed-to the West Kootenay Power and Light installation at Waneta; but when after completion it was found that in southeastern British Columbia there was a 75,000 kilowatt surplus of power, the government stepped in and refused the right to export that power to the United States.
Is there a line of demarcation between the resource of water and the resource of electrical energy, or are they one and the same because water is the raw material of hydroelectric energy? Sir, I sincerely hope that I have not made confusion worse confounded. I have tried to raise some of the problems as I see them, and to give my honest interpretation of what is in the mind of the provincial government after my talk with the premier and the minister of lands and forests of that province.
I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying, Mr. Speaker, that I am 100 per cent in support of the principle of the bill we are now discussing. I believe it is high time there was a greater understanding on the part of the federal government and a greater interest in the development of local resources for the national good; that there was a greater interest not only in the protection of our resources but also a greater interest in the development of our resources in the various provinces of Canada. It is because I am so much in support of what I am convinced is the purpose behind this bill that I would hate to see it bog down and the issue become even more confused. Because these present difficulties, problems and misunderstandings, perhaps, have not been cleared away I sincerely hope that we shall hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) before this bill leaves this house on second reading, so he can clarify a number of the problems and points I have brought up.
In conclusion may I say I feel that both governments have been wrong in carrying on a press warfare. I hope, and I think we will all agree, that in the future, instead of going after each other hammer and tongs we shall make an effort to get together and talk things over and see if provincially and nationally we cannot get together in the interests not only of our province, its industries and its resources, but the general good of the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to commend the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and also the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) on the approach which they have adopted in this dangerous situation. The remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East must have impressed even the most hotheaded among the bureaucrats in Ottawa that it is a good thing to be just a little cautious, and that you cannot override the provinces. Of course the Dominion of Canada, with all its might, could override the provinces, but in so doing it would destroy the Dominion of Canada, which is a very serious matter and should give pause for a great deal of thought.
I will just say this in leaving the hon. member for Vancouver East. He spoke just as I would expect him to speak, as a socialist, in favour of this bill. I, as a Social Crediter, will oppose the bill and the principle of the bill, because I believe that the hon. member for Vancouver East had just as much sense about how to govern British Columbia when he was in the British Columbia legislature as he has now when he is in the House of Commons at Ottawa. Consequently, he could have governed in British Columbia just as well as he can possibly do in Ottawa.
Why then take the power and authority away from the province, which will do the job well, and put it in the hands of the dominion which may or may not do the job well? That is the great point that has to be dealt with. I referred to that last night to some extent in my little discursions into Rhodes scholarships and the like.
The cause of Bill No. 3, which is before the house at the present time, would strongly appear to be the Castlegar dam project proposed by British Columbia. I desire to get away entirely from political considerations and try to shed light and not heat on the situation. It will be my endeavour in this speech to present to the house and to Canadians all across our country a readily understandable picture of the Castlegar dam, sometimes called the Kaiser dam project. What is the nature of it? What is the purpose of it? What are the motives behind the proposal of it?
Details in my remarks will be based upon the plan as outlined by Mr. R. E. Sommers, British Columbia minister of lands and forests and minister of mines in his radio address over radio station CBU Vancouver on November 29, 1954. By doing that, I shall be able to keep away from all these extraneous

International Rivers
things which the hon. member for Vancouver East injected into the discussion, thereby causing confusion. My object is to keep the issues clear.
The proposed Castlegar dam is to be located at the outlet of Arrow lakes, British Columbia. The general idea behind the project may be briefly stated thus: The British Columbia government, through the use of this dam, proposes to store 3 million acre feet of high water in the Columbia river and let that water down the Columbia into the United States in times of low water to help maintain production in certain United States hydroelectric plants, and to receive, as compensation, power to the value of some $840,000 per year for 50 years. In effect it means the saving of the 3 million acre feet of water normally running to waste, and selling that water to the United States people for at least $840,000 to help pay off British Columbia's heavy provincial debt.
The Arrow lakes constitute a hundred mile long enlargement of the gigantic Columbia river in the interior of British Columbia. At the outlet of the Arrow lakes is the town of Castlegar, located on the banks of the Columbia river near what are known as the Castlegar narrows. Past Castlegar there flows each year through these narrows down to the United States border, a distance of some 25 to 30 miles, a huge volume of Canadian water which is running to waste as far as Canada is concerned, a waste of water to Canada, a waste of hydroelectric power, too. If that water comes down in times of high water the United States cannot use it, and it is then a waste to the United States and to the whole North American continent. I hope that matter will be borne strictly in mind by all people dealing with this matter.
What can the British Columbia government do? What could any group of people in the house do? What could you do? What would you do? What can the British Columbia government do to salvage some of this waste water? Could that government build a dam at Castlegar or further down, generate electric power and use it in those parts of the province? The facts available to the British Columbia government seem to prove that the terrain at Castlegar is not stable enough to support a high crest dam. This seems to be a fact that most people who talk about this project too hastily do not know.
Can nothing be done about this waste? The British Columbia government think that something might be done. If a low-level dam could safely be built at Castlegar and it was high enough and strong enough, then the water in the Arrow lakes could be backed
up and the level raised high enough to store an estimated 3 million acre feet of water to be held there to be let run downriver in times of low water. If this can be done then perhaps that stored-up water which is running to waste now could be backed up to supply hydroelectric generating plants downriver in the United States at periods when they need that water in order to keep those plants running at the most profitable rate. The return to British Columbia for that water under this proposal is that the United States shall grant British Columbia payment in terms of power and not money.
The British Columbia government believes, and has believed, that the evidence available justifies them in exploring the possibility. I hope it is not unconstitutional to explore possibilities! In order to find the most satisfactory and economical way in which to get the necessary exploring done, they studied the matter for some time. Finally a United States company offered to undertake the job of exploring on what looked like rather attractive terms. This company is the Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation.
This United States corporation, after lengthy negotiations with the British Columbia government-as all negotiations in connection with this project have been lengthy and careful; as careful as would have been the case with any dominion government group, notwithstanding the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) with all his wisdom- this Kaiser company after lengthy negotiations finally arrived at an agreement with the British Columbia provincial government.
The company finally agreed, first, to explore the physical and economic feasibility of building such a low-level dam at Castlegar narrows at the outlet of the Arrow lakes and second, in case the exploration satisfied both the province and the company as to the feasibility of the project, to construct at Castlegar a low-level dam. There are two distinct phases to the contract, two distinct kinds of jobs to be done: First, exploring, and second, constructing.
The corporation agreed to explore on the following terms-may I draw attention to the great care which the British Columbia government has exercised in that agreement. They got an agreement just as good as the Minister of Fisheries could get: First, the corporation would post a bond of $125,000. Second, they would proceed immediately with test borings, geological surveys, field engineering and other engineering work for the purpose of determining the feasibility of the project.

Third, they would spend not less than $100,000 before March 1, 1955-I understand there has been a change in that date because of circumstances over which no one had any control-or a proportionate amount of the $100,000 if the project were deemed unfeasible before March 1. Fourth, they would furnish to the province a certified statement containing a complete record of all expenditures. Fifth, they would forfeit the corporation's $125,000 bond if they failed to comply with all the provisions of the agreement. Even a Rhodes scholar could not do any better than that!
The agreement to explore was signed on September 17, 1954. Note that it is an agreement only to explore. All the silly outbursts that have been heard from various members of this government occurred after this agreement to explore, not construct, had been signed. I do not recall in the history of Canada such recklessness in pronouncements by ministers of the crown. The British Columbia government did not go so far as has been contended in signing that agreement on September 17.
The corporation, if it were judged feasible by both principals, agreed to construct the Castlegar dam on the following terms: First, the corporation would incorporate a Canadian company under the laws of British Columbia. Second, it would obligate its Canadian company to make application for a licence under the provisions of the water act, to which reference has already been made today, it being recognized that such licence if granted would permit construction of the works. Third, it would at the time of the application recognize entitlement to be heard to all those whose rights would be affected and to anyone representing public interests. Fourth, in case the licence is granted to and accepted by the Canadian company, then the Canadian company or the corporation will be committed to deposit forthwith a further sum of $125,000 as a performance bond. There is caution. There is nothing there to get awfully excited about, to call it cockeyed and that kind of thing. Fifth, it would commence the construction of the Castlegar dam on or before August 1, 1956; sixth, complete the dam on or before August 1, 1959. An orderly development all the way through! No minister of fisheries nor any other person in this parliament could do any better.
The province of British Columbia agreed that when the storage dam is completed, under the provisions of the water act they will issue a final licence to the company covering a term of 50 years. See how carefully everything has been done. There is provision for renewal of such term for such
International Rivers
period and subject to such conditions as the province and the company may agree upon. A person would think that the government out there had bartered away half of British Columbia to hear some of these reckless people talk.
These conditions would also be included in any conditional licence issued. You will notice that there is no loophole anywhere. In return for these rights the company agrees: First, to deliver to the province energy to the amount of 20 per cent of the kilowatt hours which could be generated at downstream plants of the federal government of the United States from the net storage waters created by the storage dam. That is specific, is it not? This 20 per cent is calculated to be some 42,000 kilowatt hours annually.
Second, the company agrees to deliver to the province of British Columbia 20 per cent of all energy that might from the net storage of water rendered possible by the dam be generated in such additional dams with generating facilities as may be constructed downstream, the marketing agency for the energy generated by which is the Bonneville power administration. As has been brought out this afternoon that agreement is absolutely ironclad. The figure of 20 per cent is not final, but it demonstrates how carefully everything was planned in British Columbia. The government is free to negotiate further before agreeing to a final figure. Everything has been done to protect the interests of the people of British Columbia.
There are indications that further benefits might accrue to British Columbia beyond the
42,000	kilowatts. There is a strong possibility that British Columbia might obtain a 60 to 70 per cent load factor on the 42,000 kilowatts delivered, in any agreed period. Based upon the 70 per cent load factor this would give British Columbia an additional 18,000 kilowatts.
What are the financial advantages to British Columbia? First there is the value of the kilowatts. We have 42,000 kilowatts at $20 per kilowatt-which is a conservative figure-which would amount to $840,000. Second, there are the taxes on the dam which are estimated to amount to $275,000 a year. That would provide a clear profit annually of at least $1 million for the province of British Columbia.
This is the kind of management that enables a Social Credit government to get out of debt! It is reported that the federal government-and I emphasize this is a report -has advanced a proposal known as a 50-50 agreement between the province and the Kaiser corporation. The minister is here and he can correct me if I make any mistakes.

I am not sure I have all the facts here, but I have made some progress since I started a week ago. To return to this reported arrangement, I believe any such 50-50 arrangement with the province of British Columbia would mean that the province or the storer would have to build and maintain the dam, a fact which not so very many people recognize. The Kaiser corporation would pay the province compensation for the stored water, and that compensation would amount to 50 per cent of the power generated with that water.

I appreciate the minister's intervention, and I am anxious to obtain all the information I can get. This is a very serious question, and I have no desire to make any mistakes. I do not want to have the same ghastly record as that built up by some members of the cabinet over the past three months. However, I have already pointed out that it had been reported that the federal government has advanced this proposition, and I am dealing with this proposition. If there is no such proposal then my remarks are naturally cancelled out.

Now, I will just repeat what I have said so everyone will get it straight. In the case of the 50-50 proposition, as I understand it, British Columbia would pay $30 million for building the dam. That money at interest of 5J per cent would cost $1,650,000 a year. Operation and maintenance of the dam would cost $350,000 a year. The annual cost to the province at that rate would be $2 million a year, going on and on. This would be a demonstration of how governments, other than Social Credit governments, get into debt.
On the basis that 20 per cent of the power generated would be 42,000 kilowatts, the province receiving 50 per cent of the power generated would get 105,000 kilowatts per year. At $20 per kilowatt this would give
105,000	x $20 or $2,100,000 annually; but the annual cost to the province would be $2 million. Thus the net financial return to the province would be only $100,000. But if the Kaiser corporation built the dam the province would have collected $275,000 as taxes. Such taxes would be lost if the province owned the dam. Thus by using the 50-50 device reported proposed by Ottawa the province would sustain a net loss of $175,000 per year, and at the end of 50 years would still be in debt for the $30 million estimated capital cost of the dam.
It will therefore be seen that there is no need to bring in control from Ottawa in order to have good management of the province's affairs.
Some important questions have arisen out of the controversy which has taken place on this question. The first is, will this Castlegar or Kaiser low-level dam upset the present economy of Arrow lakes? British Columbia's official answer to this is:
Water will be stored only at such heights as will not damage existing communities, farm areas, and land transportation.
This argument has been advanced by many people, though I am not going to refer to any individual in particular. I am trying to keep names out of this except, of course, for that of the Minister of Fisheries and I am quite happy to mention him because I understand he is a Rhodes scholar.
The second question is, will the application of the principle involved in this Kaiser dam project tend to establish a vested interest in the United States? It is recognized that the dominion government always has to be careful to see to it that a vested interest is not established in the United States because of possible complications in the future. But is there that danger of establishing a vested interest with regard to water or power in this instance? The answer is no. The water

concerned is already running into the United States and going to waste. How can we establish a vested interest when the U.S. already are getting all the water?
Power is not going to be exported. The hon. member for Vancouver East, although he displayed a fine knowledge of the matter, still seemed to have the idea that power was going to be generated in British Columbia and exported to the United States. Such is not the case. The water is to be allowed to go downriver and the power is to be generated in the United States and probably sold there, because there is little likelihood of it being sold in British Columbia for the simple reason that British Columbia could not at the present time absorb that power in that particular area. There is no chance of establishing a vested interest with respect to water and power which could be of any real danger.
Furthermore the entire agreement will be terminated at the end of 50 years, at which time the province will be completely free to renegotiate; and that again obviates the possibility of there being any vested interest. I hope that at the end of this period the province of British Columbia will be still running its own affairs and will be guided by men just as wise as those who are guiding its policies today.
The third problem is, should British Columbia develop the Kaiser corporation project of storing water in the Arrow lakes before certain other projects for producing power in that particular area of British Columbia? For example, such projects as Waneta dam No. 1 and Waneta dam No. 2, Murphy creek, and Mica creek. There is much talk about the advisability of developing one or other of those projects. Let us examine them. The answer is no in each case. Waneta No. 1, capable of greatly increased power production, has not been further developed because there is not in that area enough market for power to justify the expansion of the plant or of its production. That just punctures some balloons of imagination quite thoroughly.
Waneta No. 2 cannot possibly be developed until after Waneta No. 1 attains full development. That spoils the fun again for a lot of the boys, does it not? As to Murphy creek: from the hydro engineers' standpoint, Murphy creek should be developed only after Waneta 1 and Waneta 2 have been developed to full realization of their potential, and their resultant power shall have been purchased in British Columbia. It cannot be purchased outside because the dominion government prohibits the export of electricity. Just look at the corner that puts a lot of the wise boys at Ottawa in!

At the present time there is already in that area of British Columbia-as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said-a surplus of 75,000 kilowatts that cannot as yet be marketed. Then how could you conceivably develop Waneta No. 2 or Waneta No. 1 with that surplus of power already in the general district? The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) points out that the wise boys here are allowing that 75,000 kilowatts to go to waste.

Fourth, such a Murphy creek dam would create a reservoir that would distress the presently expanding settlements and industries in the vicinity of Castlegar. Those are enough considerations to make a person a little bit hesitant about advocating the Murphy creek dam too energetically.
It is agreed by British Columbia authorities that the Murphy creek project is one that ought to be constructed when market conditions in British Columbia warrant it and not until then, but that at present Murphy creek dam should be deferred. Again I think that the detailed exposition of the legal and constitutional questions could be more satisfactorily dealt with when specific clauses of the bill are studied in committee. I agree entirely that consideration in committee will help clarify the position, but this is an important aspect of the question and it might be useful if I made a few remarks about the constitutional question at this time.
I believe it is generally recognized, sir, that water and all its uses are of tremendous importance in a country. One of its important uses is for the production of hydroelectric power. That is the most obvious use. I might mention the shortage of good and cheap sources of waterpower in Canada. I might mention its enormous value in industrial growth wherever it is available. I might mention also, in spite of what the hon. member for Lethbridge said this afternoon, the constantly increasing requirements, both in Canada and in the United States, for water power. Because of such importance, it is obvious that any water in a river that crosses an international boundary may be of great interest to countries on both sides of the boundary. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the other night when he spoke on the question.
The boundary waters treaty of 1909 dealt with certain aspects of waters of an international character. It dealt mainly, though, with boundary water. It also dealt with anything that could affect the level of a river where it crosses a boundary. That is article 4 of the treaty. It also deals with the possibilities of damage to downstream interests in another country. That is article 2. In short, I believe the fact that water crossing a boundary may be of interest on both sides of the boundary has been recognized for over 40 years under that treaty.
International Rivers
The boundary waters treaty did not deal with matters relating to the division of jurisdiction in Canada as between provincial and federal governments. I hope this will satisfy the hon. member for Lethbridge. The fact that it was based on the recognition of the broad national and international importance, not only of boundary waters but of waters crossing a boundary, seems to me to be relevant in considering any argument that the waters in such rivers are purely a matter of provincial concern.
It is perfectly clear that an action that affects the flow of water downstream in another country cannot possibly be a matter of purely provincial jurisdiction. When it affects the waters on the other side of the boundary, how can it be solely a matter of provincial jurisdiction? It is surely a matter of international importance and it is clearly a matter of national concern since it has consequences, as I said, not only inside the country, but outside the country.
I come now to the bill itself, Mr. Speaker.
I wish to draw the attention of the house to an important point that could cause misunderstanding and which has caused misunderstanding. I realize it is really a case of misunderstanding after listening to the hon. member for Lethbridge. I believe that misunderstanding may have been created by the short title of the bill which is "International Rivers Act". It might give the implication that the legislation applies to all aspects of international rivers. That might be the reason why the hon. member for Lethbridge asked this afternoon if the federal government was going to have jurisdiction over all our international rivers. That is not what this bill is for. Perhaps I had better read the bill slowly so that hon. members may understand it.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Then I will not do it. The hon. member for Lethbridge said that this bill asserts general jurisdiction with regard to rivers as such and covers all works on any international river. An examination of the bill-I shall not read it-will make clear that that is not the case. The bill does not confer jurisdiction with regard to any and all works on any and all international rivers. It covers only a certain limited type of work on such rivers.
It covers works that do both of two things; first, that increase, decrease or alter the natural flow of an international river, and- note that the word is "and" not "or"-second, interfere with, alter or affect the actual or potential use of the international rivers outside Canada. In short, the bill does not deal

International Rivers
with international rivers as such; it does not deal with all works, it deals only with works that alter the flow of the river and also affect the use of the river outside of Canada. Those are two conditions which have to be in existence in order that we have jurisdiction under Bill No. 3.
If a work does not have consequences outside of Canada it is not covered by the bill. The Saint John river was mentioned the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). Let us suppose that a dam were to be built at Beechwood, New Brunswick, to produce power: that dam would not be covered by the bill because it would not affect the use of the river outside of Canada. Consequences of the works outside of Canada are essential before any work becomes subject to the bill.
It seems to me that works of a character referred to in the bill are obviously of national importance and interest. The British North America Act recognizes that there can be works of such character and it makes specific provision for them. I should like to refer to section 92 which was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch).
Section 92 (10) assigns local works and undertakings to provincial jurisdiction. It reads:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:-
c. Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
What has been done in this present bill has been to apply the provisions of section 92 (10) (c) to the category of works which are clearly for the general advantage of Canada. Such declaration is contained in the legislation, I think it is clear that there can be no doubt as to the constitutional validity of the bill. What it does is to apply the specific provisions of the British North America Act to the category of work that by definition must have consequences that are of national concern.
While the constitutional position is thus unassailable, to my mind it can be argued that the works involved have important effects outside of Canada and thus they cannot be said to be of a local character.
To my mind it can be argued that the works involved in the legislation and the purpose toward which the legislation is directed are by their very nature outside of provincial jurisdiction. Not only are they under federal jurisdiction because section
[Mr. Lesage.l
92 (10) (c) is applied to this bill, I will go as far as to say that because of their character and purpose the works provided for under the bill are not of a provincial character. The works involved in the legislation and the purposes toward which the legislation is directed are by their very nature outside of provincial jurisdiction and within federal jurisdiction.
As to the works, I have pointed out already that they must have consequences outside of Canada; not just outside the province, but outside of Canada. As I said, such works cannot by definition be local works and undertakings. They cannot possibly be deemed to fall within the limits of property and civil rights in a province, because they affect property and civil rights, not only outside a province but outside of Canada. In short, I believe that the works covered by the bill are not things that are local or provincial in character.

Looking beyond the works themselves, the purposes toward which the legislation is directed are obviously national in character. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra referred to this last Friday, and I should like to quote from page 875 of Hansard as follows:
I believe the whole foundation of the bill is contained in the words-I cannot refer to a section, Mr. Speaker, but these words are used-"developing the water resources in the national interest". That is what this bill aims to do, develop the water resources of Canada in the national interest.
The hon. member was entirely correct. That is the purpose of the bill, namely, to develop and utilize the resources of Canada in the national interest. That purpose will be the test of the measures taken under this legislation. That purpose is obviously a national purpose and is not a local or provincial one.
In short, sir, the works covered by the legislation are works that are national in interest and character and the purposes behind the legislation are purposes in the national interest. I do not wish to go into the legal aspects of the matter more fully at this time but I think it is clear beyond doubt that the character, scope and purpose of this legislation come entirely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. That legislation does not in any way infringe upon or invade any area that is properly of provincial jurisdiction.
The introduction of this bill marks to my mind a forward step in recognition of our water resources and the necessity for safeguarding them in the same manner as was envisioned by the United States, first, in the appointment of its federal power commission which, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has already mentioned, holds authority over the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements in that country; and secondly, in the formation of the Columbia interstate compact commission by which the individual states in the basin have united to gain the greatest over-all benefit from the water resources of this river system.
In order that no sacrifice of our allimportant water resources may be made
International Rivers
through too much emphasis being given to a short-range view, such as advocated by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) this afternoon, rather than the farsighted appraisal submitted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I cannot emphasize too strongly the immediate need for this house to give its favourable consideration to Bill No. 3, which is designed to afford to the water resources of Canada a measure of protection similar to that now given the water resources of the United States.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I would first like to refer to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) as to the purpose of this bill and which is reported at page 870 of Hansard for February 4 as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to enable the Canadian government to ensure that the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements are carried out in an orderly manner and in the national interest.
But, Mr. Speaker, I submit that is the aim of all provincial governments in Canada. I submit also that the people of Canada under provincial governments are quite willing and able to develop their natural resources in the best interests not only of their own provinces but of Canada as a whole.
I would not for one moment suggest that wisdom and ability are concentrated in the federal cabinet or government. There is no evidence whatsoever of any unwillingness on the part of any provincial government to carry out the avowed purpose of this measure as outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
That leads me to the conclusion that I must look beyond the remarks of the minister to find out the exact purpose behind this measure. It has already been stated here that there is a certain political flavour to this measure due to the difference in political thought between the provincial and federal governments. In this regard I would refer to the remarks of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage). The minister referred to the "party of the province of British Columbia" when he corrected himself, having said, "the government of British Columbia". That would indicate to me that he himself believes this is more

International Rivers
a political battle and has less to do with the protection of our resources throughout Canada so that they be developed "in an orderly manner and in the national interest."
I agree the minister has some reason for his statement, and justification may be found in some of the press reports which have been quoted in this house. But in regard to the willingness or lack thereof of the provincial government to develop natural resources in the best interests of all Canadians, I think it is worth bringing to the attention of this house again the fact that General McNaugh-ton himself suggested that a committee should be set up to investigate the Columbia river basin and its power potential. The provincial government agreed to do so and also agreed to put on that committee the men recommended by General McNaughton.
It might also be worth recalling that the provincial government carried out the recommendation for a joint project by provincial and federal authorities to investigate the Columbia river basin. It seems to me that the province of British Columbia has cooperated to the fullest extent with regard to this matter.
I understand the Mica creek proposition is possibly 10 or 15 years away. What is the Mica creek dam going to do to rivers across the border? By looking at the map and obtaining some figures on the rate of flow that reaches Columbia river below the Mica creek dam it is evident that the Mica creek dam is going to do exactly what the proposed Kaiser dam will do, and that is regulate the flow.

speechtext:
Other members who have already spoken in this debate, Mr. Speaker, have emphasized the

far-reaching implications of the particular bill that is before us. I might say that I am in full agreement with those statements concerning the wide implications of this measure. We are all aware, I think, of the importance of water resources to the economy of our nation. I believe we are all desirous that those resources be developed in the best interests of the people of Canada as a whole. When we consider this bill before us, therefore, I feel we can at least credit ourselves with sincerity of purpose and consider the matter as it is presented to us.
I believe the importance of this measure is emphasized by the fact that the government has seen fit to place it in a top priority position on the agenda of the house. We could possibly feign innocence and ask why the measure was placed there, but I do not believe anyone is under any illusion as to the purpose in introducing it now. The hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) have presented the situation to us. There has been no attempt on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to prove that the purpose of the measure was not to block construction of the Kaiser dam.
I believe there is one phase of the problem that is now before us that is of special interest, and I want to deal with it now. I refer to the hydroelectric potential of the province of British Columbia. We have had a great many submissions in regard to the development of power, but reading from "Water Powers of British Columbia", which is published by the department of lands and forests, I find the following on page 9:
With the establishment and growth of industries in British Columbia came concurrent need and demand for development of power. From 1910 to 1920 the amount of developed horse power rose from 65,000 to 310,000. During the next 10 years, by 1930, the figure had more than doubled to
630.000	hor- e power, and, despite the depression years, had risen to 789,000 in 1941.
I continue to quote:
The 5 years since 1947 have resulted in the most spectacular growth in the province's history, with an increase from 864,000 horse power to 1,390,000 horse power. Developments already under construction will provide an additional 2 million horse power, emphasizing the important part being played by water power on the economy of the province.
I understand that at the present time the production of power stands at approximately
2.173.000	horsepower. And so, as we consider this, and as we think of the developments in British Columbia, we can understand how important and how significant this bill is in our particular situation. We think of the tremendous possibilities of the Columbia system. We find that figures are given to us
International Rivers
indicating that the Waneta No. 1 dam can be brought up to its full capacity of 500,000 horsepower, that Waneta No. 2 can be developed giving an additional 500,000 horsepower, that the potential Mica at-site power is
800,000	horsepower, that the Downie creek at-site potential is 500,000 horsepower, and so on. There are several other developments all of which greatly increase the power development in that particular area.
And, in connection with development, I have here an article from the Montreal Gazette of January 12, 1954, which states:
British Columbia's undeveloped hydro potential is about as large as the total hydro power now developed in Canada, Dr. Albert E. Grauer, president of the British Columbia Power Corporation Ltd., said here yesterday.
Of course this was said about a year ago. It continues:
Dr. Grauer told the Canadian Club of Montreal that the Columbia river in the southeastern part of the province and in the United States "permits perhaps the world's outstanding hydro development."
This project, he said, has "an eventual installed capacity of close to 50,000,000 horsepower."
And then again, in the Ottawa Journal of March 1 of last year we have reference to the construction of the proposed Mica creek development, where it says:
The British Columbia scheme envisions a dam on the upper Kootenay river to back part of its water across a narrow gap into the Columbia river watershed. This would increase the flow on the Columbia river, where the main dam would be constructed. The estimated power development is 40,000,000,000 kilowatt hours annually, compared with the estimated 12,600,000,000 kilowatt hours annually to be secured from the St. Lawrence power project at Barnhart island.
And it goes on to say:
General A. G. L. McNaughton, chairman of the international joint commission Canadian section, supports the Canadian development as desirable for this country, and believes that the federal and provincial governments could work out arrangements for financing.
This was in connection with the Mica creek development. As we continue to consider the potential of British Columbia in the matter of hydroelectric development we think of the potential of the Fraser river. We have not heard much about it up to the present time, but there is a tremendous power potential on that river.
I have here an article headed "The Fraser River Project" from the Fraser Valley Record of December 9, 1953-which is a little outdated, perhaps. However, it says:
"As a source of energy the Fraser river must be considered the mainspring of British Columbia. Its wise exploitation represents one of the greatest and most thrilling hazards that lie ahead." These are the words of Dr. Harry V. Warren, professor of mineralogy and petrology, U.B.C., as reported by R. A. Francis writing in "Canadian Business" for October.

International Rivers
Three main dams would be the basis of the project, at Lillooet (130 feet), Moran (750 feet) and Cottonwood (250 feet). It is estimated that the Moran dam alone could develop up to 25 per cent of the total hydro power now developed in Canada. The site at Moran, according to Dr. Warren, could develop one-quarter of the capacity of all hydro plants installed in the United States between 1930 and 1950. The installed capacity of the Moran plant would be of the order of 3 million horsepower compared with 2-2 million horsepower estimated for the St. Lawrence seaway.
I should like also to call attention to a very interesting publication called A Plan for Tomorrow, issued by the dominion-provincial board of the Fraser river basin. The article is headed "Flood Control and Water Power" and states:
The Fraser is a Canadian river. Although a small portion (177 square miles) of its drainage area of 89,487 square miles lies in the United States, the Fraser river itself is contained entirely within British Columbia and, with its tributaries, comprises the greatest potential source of power in the province. Estimates of the total hydroelectric potential of the Fraser have been steadily revised upward as more and more specific information is gathered. At the present stage of investigations it appears not unreasonable to expect the total potential to approach 10,000,000 horsepower.
It goes on to designate the various areas where that power can be generated. This shows something of the potential of the Fraser river in British Columbia.
Would you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

When we think of the relative position of this Kaiser project and when we think of the potential of British Columbia, it seems to me that it is just a comparatively small link in the development of the tremendous power potential of the province that will assist rather than defeat the goal of optimum development of our natural resources.
What the Kaiser corporation gains under the proposed deal would eventually, as we have been told this afternoon, be obtained by the construction of the Mica creek dam; but they are prepared to make this investment for speedier attainment under controlled flow. In the meantime, British Columbia is going to reap the benefits of over $1 million in financial and power returns. We are also reminded of the fact that the whole plan can be renegotiated at the end of 50 years and other arrangements made, if desired.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), as reported in the Province of November 8, is supposed to have said that the Social Credit party was a new government and Ottawa let them feel their way, but he said that the time has come to answer Mr. Bennett. That is, shall I say, a very paternal attitude for the minister to take in regard to the province of British Columbia. But may I suggest that in the two and a half years or so that the British Columbia government has been in office it has felt its way farther along the path of progressive, sane and sensible government than the previous government did in 22J years.

this particular project, again the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources spoke out and said, "That is it; that is it." I did not know just how to take that. I was not sure how I should take it at that time, but it seems to me that he was implying that we should not do it because it was going to help out somebody else.
We have heard a lot about developing natural resources in the best interests of Canada. We have heard about our international obligations, how we have to get along with our friends to the south; and I do not think we should take, shall I say, a dog in the manger attitude and say, "We won't need this power just now, we do not need it ourselves, but we are certainly not going to let other fellows benefit".
I am sorry the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., (Mr. Fairey) is not in his place tonight. He was in my riding some time ago, late in November, because I have here a report which appeared in the Abbotsford, Sumas and Matsqui News of December 1. This is the report:
Liberal government in Ottawa will block the Kaiser dam deal proposed by British Columbia's Social Credit administration, because Liberal policy will always oppose "giving away any natural resources that are needed for development in Canada, in order that our youth may benefit from that resource."
I would like to ask the hon. member, Who is giving away what? Without jeopardizing future developments British Columbia is allowing the Kaiser corporation to erect a low-level dam to regulate the flow of water that goes over the border anyway. Without the investment of a dollar they will receive in return power and payments amounting to over $1 million. So I say, who is giving away what in that deal?
The hon. member for Victoria, B.C., referred to the fact that our youth might benefit from that resource. I should like to ask what the youth of Canada have reaped from 20 years of Liberal rule-unemployment, lost markets and taxation. I think our national debt now requires an annual payment of $500 million in interest. I was reading somewhere the other day that across the border someone said that if they passed along their national debt to the oncoming generation it would mean the end of ancestor worship as we know it. That is true, not only across the border but here in Canada.
