speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I must be getting soft in my old age, or perhaps it is the fact that there arrived today at my daughter's house in Vancouver our first grandson. Then again it may be the double peacemaking effect of the return of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I am going to try my very best tonight to do a little bit of peacemaking. I think the vein which this debate has taken is a bad thing for Canada, is a bad thing for British Columbia, and is a bad thing for this house.
I believe that we are dealing with very serious issues. I cannot refrain from saying that perhaps I am slipping a bit when I see the smiling face of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I have been waiting around for two whole years to make a speech on Social Credit, but I have not yet found one Social Crediter who is willing to make a speech on Social Credit. They are all ready to speak on anything under the sun but Social Credit. And so my speech is there waiting for that time when they dust it off and bring it out.
I am beginning to believe that there is only one real Social Crediter in the whole Social Credit group in this house and that is the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), for whom I have found a soft spot in my heart although I am a bit confused. A couple of years ago he used to be talking . about the international bankers, then a year
(Mr. Patterson.]
later it was the Turko-Mongolians, and now it is the Rhodes scholars. I have a bit of trouble keeping up.
When I hear my hon. friends of the Social Credit party waxing so deeply and religiously indignant about the iniquitous Liberal party trying to play politics over this Kaiser dam, my thoughts go back to my boyhood days. I was raised in a family of 13 children, eight boys and five girls, which made it about equal. I always found that when it came to an argument with a sister I never could win. I am reminded very much of Social Credit. When a fight would start my sister would run upon me like a little hell cat; she would raise her arm like this and bring the point of her elbow down on my cranium with a resounding crack, and the minute I drew my fist back to do something about it she would raise her hand and say, "Don't you dare hit a girl, you coward," and she would make her getaway.
What we are dealing with here is not the Kaiser dam but a very important national responsibility. I have heard hon. members of the group in the extreme right of the house say that what we should have is the dominion government sitting down with the government of British Columbia. I would have you remember, and I am sure the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) remembers it very well, because he sat ini on three meetings of the committee, that the committee on external affairs met last year on May 12 and 13.
We had before us to give evidence that great business statesman General McNaugh-ton. Whatever our opinions on party politics may be, every Canadian of every age and political persuasion should be glad that we have such a competent man representing us in the deliberations of the international joint commission. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) was asking the general about this business of the province perhaps going ahead and doing something which the international joint commission might not want them to do. Here is the general's answer as reported on page 174 of the evidence:
Q. The dominion government would take no part in the construction of these developments?
A. The federal government of Canada has the over-all responsibility of negotiations with the United States. It is very essential that the negotiations in regard to the benefits that come from the regulated water and controlled flow, and so on, should be settled and will have to be settled before it would be wise for the provincial government to authorize someone to go ahead and build it.
I would ask any hon. gentleman opposite whether that is a fair statement, and whether that was the framework on which we should have proceeded. That fitted in with federal

and provincial views in the over-all plan which was being conducted by our representatives at the international joint commission.
Here is an extract I would particularly draw to the attention of hon. members.
By Mr. Green:
Q. I have seen a newspaper report to the effect that the Kaiser company of the United States is planning to dam the Arrow lakes at some point. What are the actual facts about that proposal?
A. I cannot give you a great deal of information on that subject. A report came out in the newspaper under date of February 22, 1954. I had been the previous day in British Columbia for consultation with the British Columbia committee on the Columbia. I had a very bad cold and I went up north to try to shake it. I did not know about these conversations until I got back to Ottawa. Whatever announcement has been made, has been made by authority of the British Columbia government.
I would simply point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members that within one day of the time General McNaughton specifically went to British Columbia for the exact purpose of concluding these plans- and there was none of the conflict which some hon. members now say exists-an announcement was made through newspapers in British Columbia that this deal was under way.
I would further draw your attention to page 188 of that same evidence where General McNaughton made it very clear that the representatives of Canada on that international joint commission were and still are engaged in the most delicate kind of negotiation with their opposite numbers in the United States. This is his evidence as reported at page 188:
That is a contention which neither the Canadian members of the commission, the government of Alberta nor the government of Canada, speaking through their counsel, are prepared to accept. The result of that was that when this matter for the third time was put before the commission at our meeting in April (1954) in Washington, and after a very heated discussion, we indicated that we were prepared to close the reference . . .
I have read that, Mr. Speaker, simply to remind hon. members that this parliament of Canada and this government of Canada, which is the servant of parliament, has for close to 50 years had a treaty governing boundary waters, and that we have set up as our servant a Canadian section of the international joint commission.
In addition, for over ten years-I believe from 1943-that international joint commission has been studying the entire question of waterpower development on the upper Columbia and Kootenay river, and these negotiations at this very moment are at a most delicate stage, and a stage at which the slightest upset can destroy the work Canada has been doing for many years.
International Rivers
I cannot stretch my imagination to the extent displayed by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) the other day when he foresaw a second string Conservative party coming in to substitute for the older Conservative party. I frankly confess I cannot foresee the day when a Social Credit government will take power in Canada, though I frankly confess I did not foresee it taking power in British Columbia.
However, I would simply point out to Social Credit members that if the day ever came when they would take power in Canada they themselves would require the very legislation we are asking this house to pass tonight, because we are dealing with a very serious issue indeed and we require the protection this bill is designed to provide.
The issue is quite simple and it is that when we set up a Canadian section of the international joint commission to represent Canada we sought to represent not the British Columbia government, certainly not the Social Credit party; not the government of Canada as it happens to exist at the moment, but the Canada of today, the Canada of tomorrow, and the Canada for all time to come. The preservation and protection of the natural resources of Canada is our most sacred obligation and should be the primary concern of this house.
I am a little disappointed in most of my hon. friends opposite with the exception of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), who is a congenital optimist. As regards the others, I was disappointed because of the deep strain of blue-ruin pessimism which seemed to pervade their thinking.
What is the truth about British Columbia? The truth is that in British Columbia-that last best west-we have the greatest unharnessed horsepower in the entire world. Far be it from me to get into the statistical tangle indulged in by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), because I confess that after hearing him I thought he was talking about the A plus B theorem of Social Credit or something equally complicated or abstruse. I will simply content myself with the assertion that in British Columbia we have the greatest block of unharnessed horsepower in the entire world.
Any student of economics who studies the plain development of the past half century, or even reads the speeches of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), will readily see that in 1920 we had developed only 5 * 6 billion kilowatt hours, and that this has now gone up to 70 billion. Despite this massive power many hon. members, including the hon. member for Lethbridge, adopt a defeatist attitude and decline to recognize

International Rivers
the facts. They ask, "What can we do with all this power?" And reply, "Let us sell it at bargain basement rates to Mr. Henry Kaiser in the United States, or anyone else who will take it off our hands."
This attitude is beyond comprehension. Any student of economics who has studied the history of this century knows that industry goes to power. You do not take power to industry. My hon. friends then say that we cannot develop power in Canada for the benefit of Canada until we have a market in Canada for all that power.
But is it or is it not a fact that we did not have a single market in Canada large enough to absorb the enormous Kitimat development? What we did was to take industry to the power. I will make a prediction for my hon. friends and it is that, regardless of what party is in power in Ottawa, and regardless of what party stays in power in British Columbia, the time will come when we will require every kilowatt hour, every single horsepower, and all of our energy, and we will require it in Canada and in British Columbia for the benefit of British Columbia and for the benefit of Canada.
I can recall-and this makes me remember how old I am now getting-doing my little bit to bring the Liberal government into power in Ontario 22 or 23 years ago. That Liberal government of Ontario made a tremendous mistake because it thought it had too much power on hand and it took steps to get rid of the power they had on hand. Before many years were out it would have paid a king's ransom to get back that power which the provincial government so foolishly sacrificed. I therefore make the prediction that the time will come when we shall want all of our power. The best economic thinkers say that you can develop $100 worth of value and one hundred times the jobs for every one of your harnessed horsepower. The time will come when we shall need this great block of undeveloped power on the upper reaches of the mighty river Columbia which starts in Canada, then flows north in the form of a huge question mark and finally goes down into the United States. The time will come when we shall be glad to have every horsepower of that power, and every horsepower will be giving jobs in industry in this great Dominion of Canada.
To the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke (Mr. McLeod) I would say that I am astonished to hear him say that all we can do is to ship it 50 miles away across the border into the United States. He should think of that beautiful little city of Revel-stoke and those beautiful cities of his in the
upper Okanagan valley. Every one of them should have secondary industries in them with cheap power. Cheap power is the greatest factor in getting your secondary industries located. When it comes to the matter of power, I believe in Canada for Canadians. I believe that this bill makes it absolutely certain that the rug is not pulled from under General McNaughton and the international joint commission. When we send General McNaughton and the other Canadian members to the international joint commission I believe we should see that they have the tools to do a proper job for Canada and that nobody cuts the ground from under their feet or undoes their work behind their backs.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this subject tonight but in view of the fact that the Columbia basin covers the Okanagan valley, of which I am the representative, I think I should say a few words although already all the speeches that have been made have disclosed to the house the vital necessity of the development of the Columbia river basin. I think the members who have spoken have done an excellent job of showing the house what the scheme means to Canada and also what it means to British Columbia. But to my mind there are several questions which are still unanswered.
One of them is the constitutional question posed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I think that probably is the most serious one. Do we or do we not have the power to impose this bill on the province of British Columbia? I feel that the matter should either be referred to the supreme court for judgment or that the attorneys general of the various provinces should be called before the committee to disclose their point of view and the government should have their attorney general there at the same time. I think that is the only fair way to deal with the subject. Obviously there is a conflict of view or a doubt as to the legality of this bill in the minds of many members of this house.
The other question that I feel is still left unanswered is this. Why produce the bill at all at this present time, at this particular moment when British Columbia is starting to carry on its own development? I should also like to know what is the status of those projects already completed and operating in British Columbia. I would refer to irrigation projects and power projects. This bill is retroactive and can deal with them, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pointed out. What is to be their status in the future when this bill is

passed? That is something that I should like to know. I hope the committee will be told exactly of any dangers that may face them or any proposed changes in the operation of those projects, or what control is going to be exercised over these projects that up until now have lacked that control and have, to my mind, done a fairly good job. I refer especially to the irrigation projects. I feel that this bill should have been introduced a long time ago. If there was something lacking in the laws of Canada, then somebody has been slack on the job in not finding it out before now.
I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) the other night bringing in politics. As reported at page 886 of Hansard he said: My great opposition to the bill is that I believe it is nothing more or less than a political instrument used by the government to thwart the province of British Columbia in a development which the people have a right to expect.
Mr. Speaker, I would hate to think that assumption is correct. It is true that the production of the bill now gives ground for that assumption and possibly the present government is to blame for it. It is something that should have been settled, as I pointed out, years ago. Then this assumption would not be made at the present time because it coincides with the efforts of the British Columbia government to develop this particular project.
To my mind it is too vital and important a subject to play politics with. I do not feel that the Social Credit government should take umbrage at the action of this government because they are not the first government of British Columbia that have been turned down on an application for a similar project. There was an instance some years ago and it was not a Social Credit government.
We in the Okanagan valley are greatly interested in this matter. We know the value of water. As a matter of fact, we live in an area that would be a wilderness but for the control of water for irrigation and we know what more water and more conservation could still do for us. We could easily double the acreage that we now have under fruit and vegetables. We are anxious to know what is going to happen to the water reserves of our province because with double the water used in the Okanagan we would have little surplus left for export-that is from the Okanagan river and the Similkameen river- to any state in the union.
I would point out to the house-and I should like to compliment the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) for it-the letter he sent explaining the government point of view. It is
International Rivers
completely opposed to the view placed before the house by our Social Credit friends. I think it is only fair to place it on the record. He explains the matter in five points. The first one is this:
Construction should not be planned until completion of the current survey of the Columbia river.
I think that is a fairly reasonable suggestion, Mr. Speaker, because for the last ten years the government have been making an excellent and laborious survey of the whole area and it takes in thousands of square miles; and it will probably be two more years before that work will be completed. It seems to me that if the twelve years' work carried out by this group of engineers is to be discarded entirely, we are at fault and we have been wasting money. The other point he made is this:

That point is a most excellent one. I should like to point out that the Columbia river is the fourth largest river in North America. In its basin lies possibly the greatest undeveloped potential for power in either North or South America. The Columbia river discharges 180 million acre feet annually into the Pacific. For comparison, the St. Lawrence river empties 220 million acre feet into the Atlantic. Now, I am going to quote General McNaughton on this comparison:
Head and flow combined give power, and on this aspect of comparison it is now estimated that the Columbia in Canada and the United States may eventually have an installed capacity in excess of 34 million kilowatts not including pumping power for irrigation, as compared to the St. Lawrence eventually at Sault Ste. Marie, Niagara, Barnhart, Beauharnois and Lachine, all taken together, of about 71 million.
We are just awakening in British Columbia and possibly in Canada to the fact we have a vast storage of undeveloped power in the Columbia basin. I am glad that efforts are being made to develop that power. I had hoped that there would be greater co-operation between our province and the federal government to get the most satisfactory development possible. It is for that reason I am glad this bill is to be referred to a committee where we shall have the views of expert engineers, and I hope legal experts on the legality of the proposed measure. I believe we should hear too from representatives of provincial governments, including British Columbia. In discussion we are apt to overlook the fact that other provinces are involved. I feel that British Columbia in particular should be invited to attend to give evidence, and possibly have the attorney general state their case.
It seems this dispute between British Columbia and Ottawa arose possibly through the failure of the British Columbia government to co-operate with the international joint commission. Whether it was done deliberately or thoughtlessly I do not know, but apparently that was the start of the dispute. I believe the international joint commission is operating in the best interests of the federal and provincial governments of Canada, possibly in the best interests of all Canadians. If the proposal of British Columbia to develop
TMr. Jones.]
this dam at Castlegar fits into the over-all planning, there is no reason to block the arrangement for the development by the Kaiser interests. If, on the other hand, these plans are not in the best interests of Canada as a whole or are a breach of the over-all scheme to develop the Columbia river area, then the joint commission or the government should step in.
I feel the commission is operated on that basis, to assist the provincial governments and not thwart them. I would hate to regard the commission as a political instrument. In support of the objective of the joint commission, I should like to quote from a speech made recently by the chairman, General McNaughton, in Montreal:
Meanwhile, it will be well to remember the vastness ol the issues which are being determined in the Columbia basin and the vital consequences which the decisions will have on the future of industrial development and its placement, whether in Canada or the United States. It will be well also not to forget article 2 of the treaty of 1909 and the physical fact that natural topographical advantages for the storage of water are assets just as real as are the minerals from the mines and the products of the fields and forests. Actually storage for water is far more precious than the most precious of mines, for the reason that the flow of water will go on for ever whereas minerals are a wasting asset, used up in being put to use.
Another quotation from the same speech, again bearing out the plans this body has in the interests of the whole dominion, is as follows:
In the course of my remarks-
General McNaughton says-
-I have mentioned some rather large figures of power to be generated and made available, and there is much more also at sites along the boundary at places which I have not had time to describe to you today. But, please do not think that this means there is going to be power in Canada which will be surplus and to spare. This is certainly not the case, for the most carefully made predictions show that only a comparatively short time remains until we may expect that all our economically available hydro power will be in use.
As I have indicated, much of the hydroelectric power of North America is on rivers which constitute the boundary or flow across the boundary, and so the development of this power is the concern of the international joint commission. I assure you that it is the purpose of the commission to effect arrangements between the two countries which are not only equitable but which we hope will be recognized as such by the peoples of the two countries.
Finally, he says this:
Even more important, this treaty-
Referring to the boundary waters treaty of 1909.
-seeks also for the future to dispel trouble and prevent disputes. This it does by providing, in the international joint commission, a continuing mechanism with a comprehensive set of agreed principles of general application through which any problem along the boundary, of whatever sort, not only of water, can be brought under

review at its inception and, we hope, before danger might arise that the problem might magnify and enlarge through controversy to an extent which would create issues and disputes to alarm and embitter public opinion in either country, thus making eventual solution increasingly difficult.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that is the role of the international joint commission at the moment. They should take this problem under their wing, study it carefully as to the legal and other implications, and advise what is in the best interests of the people. I would ask our friends to the left for the co-operation of the British Columbia government with the federal government in developing their joint interests. These interests are joint. Both governments are responsible for taking care of our vast inheritance of natural resources. They are both equally responsible to the future generations of this country for seeing that these resources are not wasted in any way. This calls for national planning, not localized planning or the hit and run method we have known in the past years in connection with our natural resources, chiefly pulp and paper and, I am afraid, some waterways as well.
In conclusion, I hope the bill will be given the respect it deserves in committee by inviting all the people from every province who might be concerned, and by getting the best possible legal advice to serve the committee. It should also have the benefit of the presence of General McNaughton himself, to answer some of the very interesting questions that remain unanswered.

As I say, the uncertainty should be taken out; people are uneasy about it. The St. Croix Paper Company have tour dams located at Woodlawn, Sprague Falls, Vanceboro, and Forest City. subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps I am the last person who should speak in this house on the legality of this measure. I speak only because I realize that

sometimes out of the mouths of babes and sucklings cometh wisdom. As I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the other night I was convinced of the soundness of his argument. I have checked, double-checked and rechecked because for some 24 hours I had some hesitancy with regard to the complete correctness of his statement. During the intervening days, like the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, who, in his famous statement spoke of toil, sweat and tears, I experienced toil and perspiration but not tears. In addition, I have received some extremely sound legal advice on the basis of article 2 of the waterways treaty.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, it was signed in 1909, and was a treaty between Great Britain and the United States. It has been revised on several occasions since, the last revision taking place in 1952, but article 2 has not been revised.
Under the British North America Act the dominion has jurisdiction to implement by statute all treaties made by the imperial parliament with any foreign country. In entering this debate I should like to state specifically that I am not going to deal with the multitudinous aspects that have been dealt with by speakers from the government and opposition benches with reference to power and the utilization of power. Where you have power establishments you eventually have primary and secondary industries. I am not pinpointing in any manner or form the question of the Kaiser dam. There is no doubt in the minds of many people, and particularly those of us from British Columbia, that this is the nearest thing to our hearts so far as this bill is concerned. We are concerned about the future disposition of water power in the province of British Columbia.
In the United States a treaty may be ratified by the Senate, and then it becomes a part of the law of the land; but in Canada treaties do not become law until they are ratified by statute.
We are concerned, and I particularly, as I said, with the legality of this measure. Perhaps I am simplifying this more than I should, but to me it is a problem identical with the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. They are absolutely identical. To my knowledge we have never had a protest from the province of Alberta when the question of the export of fluids and electricity has been discussed in this house. If I am right in assuming that the problems are identical, then I think it is fair to say that since the dominion government has jurisdiction with respect to the export of fluids and electricity,

it also has jurisdiction with respect to the export of the commodity which we are now discussing.
Chapter 28 of the statutes of 1911 was passed on the basis of the British North America Act. Since it is an act of the federal parliament, it may be repealed by the same authority, namely, this parliament, of which we are members. I might point out that such repeal could create difficulties-I say "could" not "would"-with the nation to the south. However, if it did, according to the information I have received, it could terminate the treaty under article 4 by giving 12 months' written notice. Although it is an imperial treaty, it is the treaty under which article 2 operates.
I presume that, since the Statute of Westminster, Canada could declare itself not bound by the treaty by giving 12 months' written notice. It therefore seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the real point that we have to deal with arises out of article 2. That is the point that the Acting Prime Minister emphasized during his speech the other evening.
Under the provision of article 2 the imperial parliament reserved to Canada and to the provinces jurisdiction and control over all territorial waters on their own side of the border. This provision does not create jurisdiction in the provinces; it reserves existing jurisdictions and rights.
As I have already stated, there have been no objections to the authority of the federal parliament to issue permits for the export of fluids and electricity. If I am right in saying that they are practically Siamese twins, then under no circumstances should there be any objection whatsoever from any province in Canada to the passage of this bill that the Acting Prime Minister introduced when he spoke last to the house. Therefore, it seems clear to me that the jurisdiction over the control of international rivers is definitely vested within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament.
I hope that when this question comes before the committee on external affairs the best legal minds will be available to that committee. Neither the province of British Columbia nor the dominion parliament wants to have come out of this debate the wrong kind of legislation. Although the province of British Columbia has a different political idea of administration from what I have, I think it is fair to state that they are primarily interested in the development of the country. They may be wrong in their attitude and approach, and certainly as far as I am concerned they are wrong, in this matter.
International Rivers
As I understand it now the agreement would give 80 per cent of the benefit to the external country with only 20 per cent to the ownership country. I think all hon. members of this house will agree that that is not a sound type of agreement. It does not conform to the usual type of enactment under the international joint commission.
I do not want to rehash any of the many statements that have been made. When this act was passed in 1909, we were then more or less a colony. That continued so until 1931 when the Statute of Westminster was passed under which we assumed co-authority with the United Kingdom parliament, equal in all things, subordinate in none.
As far as this legislation is concerned I submit that we are on sane, sound legal ground. Probably the advice the British Columbia government is receiving has not been legally sound and I am sure that they will be sufficiently good Canadians to recognize the supremacy of the dominion parliament. In fact a hint has already been given that that will be the case. Not so many days ago the provincial minister of public works stated that regardless of what the outcome might be with respect to this so-called fight between the province and the dominion-in my opinion it is not a fight, it is just a disagreement-as a good Canadian he would have to go along with the act as set down by the dominion parliament.
I think that is a tip-off we can all take with a great deal of sincerity. I think our sole purpose individually and collectively in this house is to do the best we humanly can for the Dominion of Canada. With this situation being focused as it is, we will be good Canadians first and good British Columbians second.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
This afternoon the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) spoke for a while and I began to think that we would not need any of this power in British Columbia. He almost blew a fuse. We could probably light all the bulbs in this chamber and keep them going for the next few days if we could only harness the human horsepower we have here that is going to waste from time to time. I am sure we could use it to advantage.
I take issue with this bill for a number of reasons. The first is that the bill is directed at one province only. We can talk all we want to about the Milk river in southern

Alberta, but that river practically does not run in Alberta. If it had not been for the grace of God and a couple of hills in the way it would have run down through the United States. Even that river will not come under this bill.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources said that there were 20 rivers that would be affected. I am satisfied that every hon. member in this house has the right to know the names of the rivers that are to be affected.
I take issue with the bill because it is an infringement of provincial rights set forth in the constitution. Of course that is a matter of opinion, as some individuals in the house seem to think that it comes under federal jurisdiction while others think it is a matter of provincial rights.	.
The third reason is that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in the course of the debate, proposed what I would call a "cockeyed" scheme which might well result in unlimited damage to both the internal and the external relations of this country, and might particularly affect the province of British Columbia. I will deal with that at greater length later on.
I believe it was the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) who raised the question as to the status of this project over the other projects which have already been built. It is important that this should be outlined very clearly.
I detest legislation born of expediency, and this I believe is that type of legislation. But I do not intend to develop each of these issues with respect to this bill. There are, however, one or two observations I would like to draw to the attention of the house.
The merit of this Castlegar scheme has already been outlined and I am not going to subject the house to a further discourse in that regard. Several hon. members have already devoted much time to explaining in great detail exactly what was involved, and what British Columbia could expect if she were given the authority to go ahead with the development of this project. I must confess I have as yet heard no other alternative except that suggested by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who said that he had written to the board of trade in Trail some time ago. I cannot of course criticize any such proposal until I have seen it.
However, I do not believe we should be asked to agree to a second reading of this bill until we discover what protection is offered to the people of British Columbia. That is a vitally important question. Up

until this time the British Columbia government has apparently had the authority to carry on such development and a couple of projects have already been undertaken without any governmental interference. Now it becomes expedient to stop a particular project and that is going to cost the people of British Columbia between $1 and $2 million per year unless this government comes out with a specific proposal to reimburse the British Columbia government in some particular manner.
We have heard a great deal about orderly development in the national interest. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has already admitted that the main part of the Columbia river would be affected. 1 am quite satisfied that it will be affected, but how about the little streams that run into this particular river? This is an important question for the people who live along those little streams.
For example, the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked whether it would affect tbe Mica creek dam and apparently the answer is in the affirmative. The particular location of that dam up around the top of the Big Bend is certainly some distance from the boundary itself, and the water is not running across the boundary as does the main stream of the Columbia. There are other rivers running into the dam which will naturally have some effect upon the flow of the water at the international boundary, and it is important that we discover whether they are to be affected.
We would also like to know when we are going to develop this Mica creek power plant. Are we going to wait until the federal government comes to an agreement with the United States on a 50-50 basis, as has been suggested? A 50-50 basis, as in the case of the St. Lawrence seaway project, apparently means that we get 50 per cent and the United States gets 50 per cent, but we spend $6 for every one dollar spent by the United States. To my mind this is a different type of project and it should be dealt with differently.
I would like to know who is going to issue licences and who will receive the resulting revenue. The people of Canada have a right to know. If this government is to issue licences then I imagine the fees would go to the federal authorities. But that would not make British Columbia very happy.
I am quite satisfied the people of British Columbia will feel they are being gypped out of well over $1 million if this bill comes into effect unless they get something back in return. I would ask the minister to indicate clearly at this time, before we pass this bill, 50433-67
International Rivers
whether the people of British Columbia are going to be guaranteed an amount equal to the 20 per cent plus the $275,000 in taxes and other financial returns they could normally expect if the dam were built. That province and hon. members in this house have a right to be told before a vote is taken upon this measure. I will go as far as to say that I am determined not to support this bill unless I have an answer to a few of these questions, and I would like this one answered in particular before I am called upon to vote.
There are even more important aspects of the bill than this particular economic issue, and the most significant of these, to my mind, is the question of economic nationalism as opposed to economic internationalism. In deciding whether we are going to adopt a measure of this type, which is in opposition to an agreement already drawn between a provincial authority and a company in the United States, we must bear in mind that we might possibly disrupt an economic deal between the two parties involved.
The president of the Royal Bank of Canada at a NATO meeting today had this to say: "A return to economic nationalism is a real danger." In this instance it is possibly more dangerous than most of us realize.
I know there are many hon. members inside this house and out who are not too interested in this bill because it does not affect their particular regions, but I believe this measure is vitally important to all of us and I would urge upon them the importance of studying it closely. This is not a matter of provincialism. It is a matter of internationalism and it can well affect the relations between the two countries. The late Mackenzie King had this to say. The hon. -member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) earlier today quoted from Hansard of March 9, 1944. I believe he said he was reading what Mr. Mackenzie King had to say in respect of the setting up of the international joint commission. He also had this to say which the hon. member did not read:
The Columbia is a truly international river. Any development, and particularly any power development, of the resources of the river on one side of the boundary is certain to have an effect in the other country. For this reason it is necessary that the plans for development of the river basin in one country should be adapted to those in the other.
Mr. Speaker, the Columbia river primarily affects the states of Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana, and the province of British Columbia. In the Pacific northwest, however, there is an economic block made up of British Columbia, Alberta, Montana, Idaho, Washington, Oregon and northern California. You will notice how closely those two are in-

International Rivers
tegrated; that is, the very fact that this Columbia river so materially affects the states and the provinces involved and the fact that the natural terrain in that area is of such a nature that it would be a natural form of development to develop the whole area as an economic unit, should play a most important part in our decision as to whether or not we should go ahead and adopt this measure at this time. As yet we have no assurance that this government, if the bill is passed, will go ahead and permit that development on an international basis. We hear other stories. We have certain clippings from newspaper articles. Unfortunately the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources did not earlier today have the information tabled so that we could discover for ourselves what he told the people of Trail. But I think we can take some of that from the newspaper and deal with it at a later time. One of the things I believe he mentioned was this matter of diversion. On the matter of diversion the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had this to say when he spoke on February 4 as reported at page 871 of Hansard:
. . . the government of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction and control of the use of all waters within Canada, which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary, and has the right to divert and use these waters within Canada. The United States has the same rights south of the boundary.
That is a most important statement that the minister made, when he said that the United States has the same authority south of the boundary as we happen to have north of it. Diversion is like co-operation. It is a two-way street. I have certain maps here. Unfortunately some of these things cannot be put on Hansard, but on checking the map of that particular area I find that there are two most important dams to which we have heard considerable reference in today's debate. One is Waneta No. 1 and the other is Waneta No. 2. Both of these, as the map would indicate, are on the Pend d'Qreille river just north of the boundary. There is a drop in that river of some 700 feet from the point at which the dams are constructed down to the main stream.
I wonder-I do not know-whether we have examined closely into the possibility that the Americans may, because they are so short of power, decide to dig a tunnel from that river into the main stream just south of the border. It is only a matter of 14 miles or 15 miles. We have a million horsepower in that particular area. I do not know whether it is possible from an engineering point of view. We have not been told. The

However, that is one of the questions that should be dealt with because that would automatically mean that my good friend the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) would be most unhappy because he would not have power in the Waneta dam for his use up at Trail. We have an excess of 75,000 horsepower there now, we were told earlier. Of course we have no market for it but we are told that we should not accept a sale of a commodity down south of the border even though we could well use the finances that might come from such a sale.
I maintain that from the viewpoint of public relations it is more important that we should have good international relations as far as keeping this a sound economic block is concerned, than just to go ahead and stop the building of a reserve lake as would happen here, for instance, either, for purposes of political expediency as has been charged or for other reasons. The whole thing should be examined by engineers most closely with the view of considering not just ourselves but the whole power situation on the American side as well.

MEETING OF COMMONWEALTH PRIME MINISTERS Communique
The governments of the member nations of the commonwealth are resolved to do their utmost to ease international strain. It is their aim, not only to bring any open hostilities to an end, but to promote conditions in which real peace can grow and thrive so that freedom and plenty may be enjoyed by all peoples.
Since the last meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in 1953, agreements have been reached in various parts of the world which have had the effect of removing differences and widening the area of understanding among governments and peoples. The prime ministers welcomed the settlement of the Trieste dispute. They recorded their satisfaction that, in the Middle East, the United Kingdom's differences with Egypt and Iran had been resolved. They looked forward to closer collaboration between all the countries of that area so that its economic development and the welfare of its peoples could be advanced. They welcomed, in southeast Asia, the end of hostilities in Indo-China and stressed the need for strict adherence to the conditions of the Geneva agreement and for increased welfare and stability in that area.
The prime ministers were informed that the commonwealth countries associated with the North Atlantic treaty were convinced that the early ratification of the agreements reached in London and Paris and the acceptance of federal Germany into the community of the western nations would mark an important advance towards the security and cohesion of western Europe.
The prime ministers met at a time of tension in the Far East. In view of developments which occurred during their meeting, their discussions of this problem assumed a special significance. They were united in their conviction that it was necessary that incidents should be avoided while means were sought for a peaceful outcome. They were confident that the intimate and personal discussions which they had held at this meeting would be a valuable foundation for future consultations, with one another and with other countries directly concerned, and for the development of their policies on this question.
The prime ministers noted the improvement in the outlook for world trade and prosperity which had taken place since the commonwealth finance ministers met at Sydney in January, 1954. They recognized that commonwealth countries had made a substantial contribution to this by maintaining the stability of their currencies, by continuing their development programs, in which the Colombo plan had played its part, and by expanding their production. They had also continued their progressive approach towards the widest practicable system of trade and payments, which best serves the interest of the sterling area and Canada.
The prime ministers affirmed their determination to continue these policies of economic progress. They agreed, in particular, that all commonwealth countries should strive to develop further their resources and their earning power. By these means they could best consolidate their strength and make an increased contribution to economic stability throughout the world.
The prime ministers gave anxious thought to the problems of nucleur energy. The latest discoveries confront humanity with a force which is almost beyond the capacity of man's brain to comprehend or measure. They present a choice and a challenge. Is this vast power to be developed for the benefit of man, or is it to be used to bring ruin upon the human race?
The prime ministers once again declare that their countries will never embark upon aggression. Indeed, it is their hope that, when the peoples of the world understand the magnitude of the disaster which world war would bring, all nations will shrink from violence and follow peaceful means of settling their differences. The annihilating power of the new weapons renders it imperative that sanity should prevail and that war should be prevented.
It is the aim of the commonwealth countries to work for a disarmament agreement which includes forces and weapons of all kinds and is both comprehensive and effective. Commonwealth governments have already devoted much time and thought to producing

and furthering practical plans to achieve this purpose, and two of the commonwealth countries are members of the subcommittee of the United Nations disarmament commission.
With international accord on disarmament, it would become possible to turn the vast resources of atomic energy increasingly into channels which benefit mankind. The prime ministers were informed of the progress made by the United Kingdom government in the use of atomic energy for industrial and other peaceful purposes. They looked forward to the prospects of continued close co-operation between the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries in the development of the civil uses of atomic energy.
In the course of the meeting, the Prime Minister of Pakistan informed the other prime ministers that Pakistan was about to adopt a republican form of constitution but desired to remain a member of the commonwealth. They were assured that the people of Pakistan were resolved to maintain, despite this constitutional change, their steadfast adherence to the commonwealth and their recognition of the crown as the symbol of the free association of its sovereign members. In
Commonwealth Conference a declaration issued on February 4 they signified their agreement that Pakistan should continue on this basis to be a full member of the commonwealth after becoming a republic. All the prime ministers reaffirmed that their countries would remain united as free and equal members of the commonwealth, freely co-operating in the pursuit of peace, liberty and progress.
The commonwealth is a unique association. Its countries contain a fourth of the world's population, embracing people of many races and religions. Among its members are countries of importance in all quarters of the globe. Its strength and influence in the world today are derived from this and from a common outlook which, in spite of differences of geography, religion and race, evokes a broadly similar response to most international problems of the day.
The commonwealth countries do not pursue any selfish purpose. They seek no aggrandisement and will always oppose aggression. In concert with all who share their ideals, they are resolved to do their utmost to further the cause of peace throughout the world.

subtopic: REGIONAL DEFENCE DISCUSSIONS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
While the commonwealth prime ministers were in London the opportunity was taken to hold a series of additional meetings on regional defence problems. These meetings covered the main areas in which the forces of commonwealth countries may have to be deployed in the event of war. Each was attended by representatives of those commonwealth countries whose forces might in war be operating in the particular area under discussion. Their purpose was to enable the representatives of those countries to join together in reviewing the plans for the defence of each area.
The representatives of the commonwealth countries concerned with these regional defence plans recognized that the advent of thermonuclear weapons involves fundamental changes in the strategic approach to defence problems. They agreed that the overwhelming superiority of the western powers in nuclear weapons offers at the present time the most effective and practical
assurance that world peace will not be disturbed by any deliberate act of aggression. They agreed that their defence policies should be founded on the principle that world war can be prevented if the free democracies are resolved to maintain in readiness forces sufficiently strong to deter any potential aggressor.
In Europe great progress has already been made in building up the defensive shield provided by the forces of the North Atlantic treaty powers; and the commonwealth representatives who took part in these discussions welcomed the steps which are being taken to increase the strength of those forces by a military contribution from western Germany. The defence problems of the Middle East were reviewed in the light of recent developments and agreement was reached on the basis for a new approach to defence planning in this area. Discussion of the defence problems of southeast Asia covered plans to help the countries in that

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Commonwealth Conference area, not only to resist aggression, but also to strengthen their internal security. The four commonwealth countries which are signatories of the Manila treaty took this opportunity of reviewing, in preparation for the forthcoming conference at Bangkok, progress in making that treaty an effective instrument for these purposes.
The opportunity was taken to discuss, as one element in the defence of the Manila treaty area, the security of Malaya, which is regarded by the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand as of vital importance. The strategic position of the area was clarified by these discussions and it was considered
that, in future, joint planning among the three governments and discussions with other participants in the Manila treaty would go forward effectively.
Throughout these regional defence discussions it was accepted that military plans must be concerted with other countries involved in the defence of these areas. The commonwealth countries concerned also recognized the need for the closest association with the United States in all defence measures. They agreed that on this basis regional defence planning can afford a solid foundation for the preservation of peace.
